claims.text: The anomalous stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr arises from internal residual stresses generated by local thermal-expansion mismatch.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr contains minor compositional segregation.
As-cast HfNbTaTiZr can contain two BCC regions or phases associated with Ta–Zr segregation.
HfNbTaTiZr can contain grain-boundary precipitates rich in Ta.
The relevant precipitates may be nanoscale and rich in Ta or Zr.
Local compositional heterogeneities and microphase segregation create regions with different thermal-expansion coefficients.
Differential thermal expansion between those regions generates interfacial residual stresses during heating or cooling.
The resulting residual stresses alter dislocation mobility and activation.
Altered dislocation activation changes creep and strain-hardening behavior.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses modify the measured elastic moduli and their temperature dependence.
High-temperature, long-duration homogenization will minimize local compositional variations and thermal-expansion mismatches.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, the homogenized alloy will have weaker residual-stress effects.
Homogenization will reduce or normalize high-temperature tensile yield strength.
Homogenization will reduce high-temperature creep resistance.
The elastic moduli of the homogenized alloy will vary more conventionally with temperature.
An anomalous strength plateau or unexpected hardening will be diminished by homogenization.
The proposed thermal-mismatch mechanism should dominate approximately from 600 °C to 1250 °C when segregation is present.
The proposed effect should be markedly reduced in fully homogenized or compositionally uniform alloys.
Ta-rich grain-boundary precipitation can strongly reduce elongation, potentially to nearly zero.
The as-cast baseline has reported creep behavior at 1250 °C, aging hardening at 600–800 °C, and nonstandard elastic-modulus variation from 293 to 1100 K.
